attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his Where's Your Ed At post, endorsed in the first person.

semantics.note: This takes the architecture clause out of a compound sentence. The other parts (unprofitable, unsustainable) are left to other claims. The present-perfect 'has peaked' is unhedged and correctly treated as an observation.

contract.note: The plain reading is a broad capability ceiling reached by publication. That is ordinary and fair. The January 2025 window was chosen by the evaluator but is reasonable for a present-perfect claim. Excluding pretraining-only limits from 'architecture' matters to the result but is not stretched.

evidence.note: DeepSeek's own January 2025 preprint reports steady gains from RL on a transformer model. It is a developer disclosure, not an independent evaluation, and it does not separate architecture from training method. It weighs against a ceiling but does not meet the contradiction condition.
METR's March 2025 trend data is independent, but it covers a longer period and measures whole agents, not the architecture alone. Under this historical contract it is context only.

reviews.rationale: Nothing in the packet shows a broad ceiling in January 2025. The R1 gains point the other way but come from the developer and mix training method with architecture. METR is outside the target period and measures agents. Neither side's condition is met.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his post.

semantics.note: The revision faithfully keeps both what did not limit deployment (running expense) and the claimed real limiter (not AI, not the next smartphone).

contract.note: The contract reads it as: running expense was not a binding constraint, and capability limits were. That is a fair plain reading. It rightly does not invent thresholds for 'not AI' or 'next smartphone'. Whether 'the limiter' means dominant or merely material is left open.

evidence.note: A vendor-commissioned survey reports rising concern about implementation cost and accuracy. Implementation cost is not running expense, and reported concerns do not establish a causal ranking. It is a company disclosure.
A preregistered study finds hallucination rates of 17–33% in legal tools. That shows reliability limits but does not weigh them against running expense as a cause of deployment outcomes.

reviews.rationale: No item separates inference expense from other costs or compares it with capability as a deployment constraint. The survey mixes cost concerns with accuracy concerns. The legal study shows reliability problems only. The causal ranking stays unsettled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own characterisation. His note that he said so 'at the time' does not count as evidence for itself.

semantics.note: 'At launch' follows from the surrounding sentence about OpenAI rushing to launch o1. The claim is about a past state and is correctly treated as an observation.

contract.note: Reading the claim as a September 2024 o1-preview failure, without requiring every attempt to fail, is fair. Requiring broader testing for 'not particularly reliable' is reasonable. Mapping 'o1' to the launch version is the evaluator's choice.

evidence.note: Futurism (13 September 2024) passes on social-media reports that the model sometimes failed the strawberry count, plus other errors. These are secondhand user claims with no transcript and no representative measurement.
The X post is ambiguous: it links a video of a correct answer and says others 'recreated' the issue. It shows no failed exchange and gives no model settings.
A later secondary page, since updated, says o1-preview counts correctly. Correct answers do not rule out occasional failures, and the page is not a test record.

reviews.rationale: No version-identified failed transcript or reliability measurement is in the packet. The only failure evidence is secondhand user reports. Reports of correct answers do not rule out occasional failures. Neither the support condition nor the contradiction condition is met.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his post.

semantics.note: 'Isn't coming' is unhedged, so it is a scored forecast with no deadline. The scare quotes and the hype context are recorded as ambiguity but do not make it a hedge.

contract.note: Plain reading: broadly human-level general capability. That is ordinary and fair. Non-arrival cannot support an open-ended forecast, and independent establishment of AGI would contradict it. The 'retrospective' label is odd but has no effect on the result.

evidence.note: ARC Prize (3 September 2026) reports major progress from Astra on ARC-AGI-3 but explicitly says it is not claiming AGI. That does not meet the early-resolution rule.
The AGI Society (14 September 2026) finds the evidence insufficient to conclude Astra is AGI and notes there is no accepted test. It is context, not a conclusive event.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated, so non-arrival so far cannot score the forecast. The Astra results are significant but are explicitly not certified as AGI by independent evaluators, so the early-resolution rule is not met. Unresolved.
